slides.title: Unit 1: Relations and Functions - Section 1.1: Relations
content: Topic: Introduction to Relations
Key Concepts: Patterns, Cartesian Coordinate System, Basic Concepts of Relations, Domain and Range, Graphs of Relations.
Objective: Define relation. Identify domain and range of a relation. Sketch graphs of relations.

slides.title: 1.1.1 Revision of Patterns
content: Definition: A pattern is a regularity in the world, human-made design, or abstract ideas. Elements repeat predictably.
Arithmetic Pattern: Sequences based on addition or subtraction. e.g., 2, 4, 6, 8, ... (rule: add 2).
Geometric Pattern: Sequences based on multiplication or division. e.g., 2, 4, 8, 16, ... (rule: multiply by 2).
Algebraic expressions can represent patterns (e.g., Output = 2n + 3).

slides.title: 1.1.2 Cartesian Coordinate System
content: Defined by an ordered pair of perpendicular lines (axes).
Axes: x-axis (horizontal, abscissa) and y-axis (vertical, ordinate).
Origin: Point where axes meet (0, 0).
Coordinates: Written as (x, y). The x-coordinate is the abscissa, the y-coordinate is the ordinate.
Divides the plane into four quadrants (I, II, III, IV).

slides.title: 1.1.3 Basic Concepts of Relations
content: Definition: A relation is a set of ordered pairs (x, y). It denotes a pairing between elements of two sets.
Example: 'y is greater than x' is a relation.
Domain: The set of all first components (x-values) of the ordered pairs.
Range: The set of all second components (y-values) of the ordered pairs.

slides.title: 1.1.4 Graphs of Relations (Part 1)
content: Relations can be represented graphically by plotting ordered pairs.
To graph a relation of the form y = ax + b, create a table of values, plot points, and connect.
Example: y = x creates a straight line through the origin.

slides.title: 1.1.4 Graphs of Relations (Part 2)
content: Graphing Inequalities:
- For '≤' or '≥', use a solid line for the boundary.
- For '<' or '>', use a broken line.
- Shade the region that satisfies the inequality.
Example: y > x uses a broken line and shades the region above the line.
For compound relations (e.g., y ≤ x and y ≥ -x + 2), the graph is the intersection of the two regions.

slides.title: 1.2.1 The Notion of a Function
content: Definition: A function is a relation where no two distinct ordered pairs have the same first element.
Each input (x-value) maps to exactly one output (y-value).
Can be represented by arrow diagrams, ordered pairs, tables, or graphs.
Function Notation: f(x) = y (read as 'f of x').
The Vertical Line Test: If a vertical line intersects the graph at more than one point, it is NOT a function.

slides.title: 1.2.1 Domain, Codomain, and Range
content: Domain: The set of all possible input (x) values for which the function is defined.
Codomain: The set of all possible output values.
Range: The set of all actual output (y) values.
Example: For f(x) = 3x + 4, the domain and range are all real numbers (R).
Example: For f(x) = √(x - 2), the domain is x ≥ 2, and the range is y ≥ 0.

slides.title: 1.2.2 Combination of Functions
content: Functions can be combined using arithmetic operations:
- Sum: (f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x)
- Difference: (f - g)(x) = f(x) - g(x)
- Product: (f · g)(x) = f(x) · g(x)
- Quotient: (f/g)(x) = f(x) / g(x), provided g(x) ≠ 0.
The domain of the new function is the intersection of the domains of f and g (with restrictions for the quotient).

slides.title: 1.2.3 Types of Functions
content: One-to-One (Injective): Each element in the domain has a distinct image. If f(a) = f(b), then a = b.
Onto (Surjective): Each element in the codomain has at least one pre-image in the domain.
Bijective (One-to-One Correspondence): A function that is both one-to-one and onto.

slides.title: 1.2.4 Graphs of Functions - Linear
content: General Form: f(x) = ax + b, where a ≠ 0.
Slope (a): Determines the steepness. If a > 0, increasing; if a < 0, decreasing.
y-intercept (b): The point where the line crosses the y-axis, (0, b).
x-intercept: The point where the line crosses the x-axis, found by setting y = 0.
Example: f(x) = 2x - 3 has slope 2, y-intercept -3, and x-intercept 1.5.

slides.title: 1.2.4 Graphs of Functions - Quadratic
content: General Form: f(x) = ax² + bx + c, where a ≠ 0.
Graph is a parabola.
Vertex: The turning point (h, k). Found by completing the square: f(x) = a(x - h)² + k.
Axis of Symmetry: Vertical line x = h.
Opens upward if a > 0 (minimum at vertex), opens downward if a < 0 (maximum at vertex).
Range: Depends on the vertex and sign of a.

slides.title: 1.2.4 Graphing Quadratic Functions
content: Key Steps:
1. Identify 'a', 'b', and 'c'.
2. Find the vertex using completing the square or formula h = -b/(2a).
3. Find the y-intercept (c).
4. Find x-intercepts by solving f(x) = 0.
5. Plot points and sketch the smooth U-shape.

slides.title: 1.3 Applications of Relations and Functions
content: Relations and functions are used to model real-world situations.
Linear Applications: Modeling relationships with constant rate of change (e.g., cost as a function of time).
Quadratic Applications: Optimization problems (e.g., maximum area with given perimeter, minimum product).
Graphical Solutions: Using graphs to solve quadratic equations and inequalities.

slides.title: 1.3 Optimization with Quadratics
content: Max/Min Problems: Often involve finding the vertex of a parabola.
Example: A wire of 56m is bent into a rectangle. Area A = x(28 - x) = 196 - (x - 14)².
The maximum area is 196 m², achieved when x = 14 m.
The vertex of the quadratic function gives the optimal value.

slides.title: 1.3 Solving Equations & Inequalities Graphically
content: Quadratic Equations: Solutions are the x-intercepts of the parabola.
Example: x² - 4 = 0 has solutions x = ±2.
Quadratic Inequalities:
- For ax² + bx + c < 0, solution is where the parabola is below the x-axis.
- For ax² + bx + c > 0, solution is where the parabola is above the x-axis.
Includes endpoints if the inequality is ≤ or ≥.

slides.title: Unit 2: Polynomial Functions - Section 2.1: Definition
content: Definition: A polynomial function p(x) = a_n x^n + a_{n-1} x^{n-1} + ... + a_1 x + a_0, where n is a non-negative integer and a_n ≠ 0.
Degree (n): The highest power of x.
Leading Coefficient (a_n): The coefficient of the highest degree term.
Constant Term (a_0): The term without x.
Domain: All real numbers (R).

slides.title: 2.1 Examples and Non-examples
content: Examples of Polynomial Functions:
- f(x) = 3x² - 2x + 5 (Degree 2, Leading Coeff 3, Constant 5)
- g(x) = 4x³ + x - 7 (Degree 3, Leading Coeff 4, Constant -7)
Non-examples:
- f(x) = 4x⁻² + 3x - 7 (Negative exponent)
- h(x) = 2ˣ (Variable is in the exponent)
- f(x) = √x (Not a polynomial function)

slides.title: 2.2 Operations on Polynomial Functions
content: Combining polynomials:
- Addition/Subtraction: Combine like terms.
- Multiplication: Distribute each term of one polynomial by every term of the other.
- Division: Use the long division process.
The result of these operations is always a polynomial function (except division by zero).

slides.title: 2.2 Polynomial Addition and Subtraction
content: Add/Subtract coefficients of like terms.
Example: (2x³ + 5x² - 3x + 4) + (x³ - 2x² + 7x - 1)

slides.title: 2.2 Polynomial Multiplication and Division
content: Multiplication: (2x+3)(x²-5x+6) = 2x³ - 10x² + 12x + 3x² - 15x + 18 = 2x³ - 7x² - 3x + 18.
Division: Long division process yields quotient q(x) and remainder r(x).
If f(x) = d(x)q(x) + r(x), where deg(r) < deg(d).

slides.title: 2.3 Theorems on Polynomials (Part 1)
content: Polynomial Division Theorem: For polynomials f(x) and d(x) ≠ 0, there exist unique q(x) and r(x) such that f(x) = d(x)q(x) + r(x), with r(x) = 0 or deg(r) < deg(d).
Remainder Theorem: The remainder when f(x) is divided by (x - c) is f(c).
Example: f(x) = 2x³ - 3x² + 5x - 7, divided by (x + 1). Remainder = f(-1).

slides.title: 2.3 Theorems on Polynomials (Part 2)
content: Factor Theorem: (x - c) is a factor of f(x) if and only if f(c) = 0.
Example: f(x) = x³ - x² - x + 1. f(1) = 0, so (x - 1) is a factor.
Uses: Factoring polynomials, finding zeros.
If f(c) = 0, then c is a zero (root) of f(x).

slides.title: 2.4 Zeros of a Polynomial Function
content: Zeros: The roots or solutions of f(x) = 0.
Finding zeros: Use factoring, Factor Theorem, or Rational Zero Test.
Multiplicity: If (x - c)^k is a factor but (x - c)^{k+1} is not, then c is a zero of multiplicity k.
Even multiplicity: Graph touches the x-axis.
Odd multiplicity: Graph crosses the x-axis.

slides.title: 2.4 Rational Zero Test
content: For a polynomial with integer coefficients, any rational zero p/q (in simplest form) must have p as a factor of the constant term and q as a factor of the leading coefficient.
Steps:
1. List factors of constant term (p).
2. List factors of leading coefficient (q).
3. Form all possible p/q combinations.
4. Test these values using synthetic division or direct substitution to find the actual zeros.

slides.title: 2.4 Location Theorem
content: If f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs, then there is at least one real zero of f(x) between a and b.
Useful for locating irrational roots.
Example: f(x) = x² - 3. f(1) = -2, f(2) = 1. Since signs are opposite, a zero lies between 1 and 2.

slides.title: 2.5 Graphs of Polynomial Functions
content: Properties: Smooth and continuous curve (no sharp corners, no breaks).
End Behavior: Determined by degree and leading coefficient.
- Even degree, positive leading: Up, Up
- Even degree, negative leading: Down, Down
- Odd degree, positive leading: Down, Up
- Odd degree, negative leading: Up, Down
Turning Points: Max n-1 for a polynomial of degree n.
x-intercepts: Max n.

slides.title: 2.6 Applications of Polynomials
content: Used to model problems involving area, volume, and optimization.
Example 1: Maximize area of a rectangle with fixed perimeter. Quadratic function models area.
Example 2: Maximize volume of an open-top box created by cutting squares from corners of a rectangular sheet. Volume is a cubic function.
Solve by finding the maximum/minimum of the polynomial function (often the vertex for quadratics).

slides.title: Unit 3: Exponential and Logarithmic Functions - Section 3.1: Exponents
content: Review of Exponents:
- Laws of Exponents: a^m * a^n = a^(m+n), a^m / a^n = a^(m-n), (a^m)^n = a^(mn).
- Zero Exponent: a^0 = 1 (a ≠ 0).
- Negative Exponent: a^(-n) = 1/a^n (a ≠ 0).
- Rational Exponent: a^(m/n) = (a^(1/n))^m = (n√a)^m.

slides.title: 3.1 Introduction to Logarithms
content: Definition: If a^b = c, then log_a(c) = b.
Read as 'log base a of c'.
Example: 2^3 = 8, so log_2(8) = 3.
Common Logarithm: Base 10, written as log x.
Natural Logarithm: Base e, written as ln x.

slides.title: 3.1 Laws of Logarithms
content: For a > 0, a ≠ 1, and M, N > 0:
1. log_a(MN) = log_a M + log_a N (Product Rule)
2. log_a(M/N) = log_a M - log_a N (Quotient Rule)
3. log_a(M^r) = r * log_a M (Power Rule)
4. log_a 1 = 0 and log_a a = 1.
5. Change of Base: log_a M = log_b M / log_b a.

slides.title: 3.1 Using Logarithm Tables
content: A number's logarithm = Characteristic + Mantissa.
Characteristic: The integer part, determined by the power of 10 in scientific notation.
Mantissa: The fractional part, found in the logarithm table.
Antilogarithm: The inverse process of finding a number from its logarithm.

sections.section_title: The Exponential Functions and Their Graphs

slides.title: 3.2 The Exponential Function
content: Definition: f(x) = a^x, where a > 0, a ≠ 1.
Domain: All real numbers (R).
Range: All positive real numbers (R+).
y-intercept: (0, 1).
Horizontal Asymptote: x-axis (y = 0).

slides.title: 3.2 Graphs of Exponential Functions
content: For a > 1: Increasing function, rises to the right.
For 0 < a < 1: Decreasing function, rises to the left.
The graph gets closer to the x-axis but never touches it.
The Natural Exponential Function: f(x) = e^x, where e ≈ 2.71828.

sections.section_title: The Logarithmic Functions and Their Graphs

slides.title: 3.3 The Logarithmic Function
content: Definition: f(x) = log_a x is the inverse of f(x) = a^x.
Domain: All positive real numbers (R+).
Range: All real numbers (R).
x-intercept: (1, 0).
Vertical Asymptote: y-axis (x = 0).

slides.title: 3.3 Graphs of Logarithmic Functions
content: For a > 1: Increasing function, rises slowly.
For 0 < a < 1: Decreasing function.
Natural Logarithm: f(x) = ln x.
Inverse Relation: The graph of log_a x is the reflection of the graph of a^x across the line y = x.

slides.title: 3.4 Solving Exponential Equations
content: 1. Isolate the exponential expression.
2. Take the logarithm of both sides (common or natural log).
3. Use the power rule to bring down the exponent.
4. Solve for the variable.
Example: 2^x = 20 → log 2^x = log 20 → x log 2 = log 20 → x = log 20 / log 2.

slides.title: 3.4 Solving Logarithmic Equations
content: 1. State the Universe (arguments must be > 0).
2. Combine logarithmic terms using log laws.
3. Rewrite in exponential form: log_a M = b → M = a^b.
4. Solve for the variable.
5. Check if the solution is in the Universe.

sections.section_title: Relation between Exponential and Logarithmic functions

slides.title: 3.5 Inverse Relationship
content: y = a^x and y = log_a x are inverse functions.
Graphs are reflections across the line y = x.
Domain of Exponential = Range of Logarithmic.
Range of Exponential = Domain of Logarithmic.

slides.title: 3.6 Applications of Exponents and Logs
content: Compound Interest: A(t) = P(1 + r/n)^(nt). Continuous: A = Pe^(rt).
Population Growth: P(t) = P_0 e^(kt), k > 0.
pH Scale: pH = -log[H+], used in chemistry to measure acidity.
These applications involve solving for unknown time (t), rate (k), or amount (A) using logarithms.

slides.title: Unit 4: Trigonometric Functions - Section 4.1: Radian Measure
content: Definition of an Angle: Rotation of a ray about its vertex.
Positive Angle: Anticlockwise rotation.
Negative Angle: Clockwise rotation.
Standard Position: Vertex at origin, initial side on positive x-axis.

slides.title: 4.1 Degree and Radian Measures
content: Degree: 1° = 1/360 of a revolution.
Radian: The angle subtended at the center by an arc equal in length to the radius (l = rθ).
Key Conversion: π radians = 180°.
To convert degrees to radians: Multiply by π/180.
To convert radians to degrees: Multiply by 180/π.

slides.title: 4.2 Basic Trigonometric Functions
content: Defined using the Unit Circle (radius 1, center at origin).
For a point P(x, y) on the unit circle: cos θ = x, sin θ = y.
tan θ = sin θ / cos θ.
Reciprocal Functions:
- sec θ = 1/cos θ
- csc θ = 1/sin θ
- cot θ = 1/tan θ = cos θ / sin θ.

slides.title: 4.2 Signs and Reference Angles
content: Signs in Quadrants (ASTC):
- I: All positive.
- II: Sin positive.
- III: Tan positive.
- IV: Cos positive.
Reference Angle: The acute angle formed with the x-axis. Used to evaluate trig functions for any angle.
Coterminal Angles: Angles that share the same terminal side (differ by 360° or 2π).

slides.title: 4.2 Graphs of Sine and Cosine
content: Sine Function (y = sin x):
- Domain: R, Range: [-1, 1].
- Period: 360° (2π).
- Symmetric about the origin (odd function).
Cosine Function (y = cos x):
- Domain: R, Range: [-1, 1].
- Period: 360° (2π).
- Symmetric about the y-axis (even function).

slides.title: 4.2 Graph of Tangent
content: Tangent Function (y = tan x):
- Domain: {x | x ≠ (π/2) + nπ}, Range: R.
- Period: 180° (π).
- Vertical asymptotes at x = (π/2) + nπ.
- Increasing function on each interval between asymptotes.

slides.title: 4.3 Trigonometric Identities
content: Pythagorean Identities:
- sin²θ + cos²θ = 1
- 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ
- 1 + cot²θ = csc²θ
Addition/Subtraction Formulas:
- sin(α ± β) = sinα cosβ ± cosα sinβ
- cos(α ± β) = cosα cosβ ∓ sinα sinβ

slides.title: 4.3 Double and Half Angle Identities
content: Double Angle:
- sin 2θ = 2 sinθ cosθ
- cos 2θ = cos²θ - sin²θ = 1 - 2sin²θ = 2cos²θ - 1
- tan 2θ = 2tanθ / (1 - tan²θ)
Half Angle:
Sign depends on the quadrant of θ/2.

slides.title: 4.3 Solving Trigonometric Equations
content: 1. Isolate the trigonometric function.
2. Use identities to simplify.
3. Determine the reference angle.
4. Find solutions in the specified interval.
5. Add the period to find all solutions.
Example: Solve 2cosθ - 1 = 0 → cosθ = 1/2 → θ = π/3, 5π/3.

slides.title: 4.4 Applications of Trigonometry
content: Angle of Elevation: The angle from the horizontal upwards to an object.
Angle of Depression: The angle from the horizontal downwards to an object.
Solving Problems: Set up a right triangle. Use SOH CAH TOA.
Example: From a 40m cliff, the angle of depression is 60°. Find the distance to the object.

slides.title: Unit 5: Circles - Section 5.1: Symmetrical Properties
content: Definition: A circle is a set of points equidistant from a fixed point (center).
Line of Symmetry: Any diameter is a line of symmetry.
Chord Theorems:
- The line from the center to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to it.
- The perpendicular from the center to a chord bisects it.
- Equal chords are equidistant from the center.

slides.title: 5.2 Angle Properties of Circles
content: Central Angle: Vertex at the center. Measure equals its intercepted arc.
Inscribed Angle: Vertex on the circle. Measure is half its intercepted arc.
Theorems:
- Inscribed angles that intercept the same arc are equal.
- Thales' Theorem: An angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle.
- Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary (sum to 180°).

sections.section_title: Arc length, perimeters and areas of segments and sectors Arc length

slides.title: 5.3 Arc Length and Sector Area
content: Arc Length: s = rθ (θ in radians) or s = 2πr * (θ/360°).
Chord Length: l = 2r sin(θ/2).
Area of Sector: A = (1/2)r²θ or A = πr² * (θ/360°).
Perimeter of Sector: 2r + arc length.
Area of Segment: Area of sector - Area of triangle (formed by the chord and radii).

sections.section_title: Theorems on angles and arcs determined by lines intersecting inside, on and outside a circle.

slides.title: 5.4 Angles from Intersecting Lines
content: Intersecting Chords (Inside): m∠ = 1/2 (sum of measures of intercepted arcs).
Intersecting Secants/Tangents (Outside): m∠ = 1/2 (difference of measures of intercepted arcs).
These theorems allow calculation of angles formed by lines interacting with a circle.

slides.title: Unit 6: Solid Figures - Section 6.1: Prisms & Cylinders
content: Prisms: Two parallel congruent bases, lateral faces are parallelograms.
For a Right Prism: LSA = p*h, TSA = LSA + 2BA, V = BA*h.
Cylinders: A prism with circular bases.
For a Right Circular Cylinder: LSA = 2πrh, TSA = 2πr(r+h), V = πr²h.

slides.title: 6.2 Pyramids and Cones
content: Pyramids: Polygonal base, triangular faces meeting at an apex.
Regular Pyramid: Regular base, congruent lateral faces.
For a Regular Pyramid: LSA = (1/2)pl, V = (1/3)BA*h.
Cones: Circular base, lateral surface meeting at an apex.
For a Right Circular Cone: LSA = πrl, V = (1/3)πr²h.
Cross-Section: Area ratio = (distance from vertex / height)².

slides.title: 6.2 Spheres
content: Definition: A solid where all points on its surface are equidistant from a center.
Great Circle: A cross-section that passes through the center.
Hemisphere: Half of a sphere.
Formulas: SA = 4πr², V = (4/3)πr³.

slides.title: 6.3 Frustums of Pyramids and Cones
content: Definition: The part of a pyramid or cone between the base and a parallel cross-section.
For a Regular Frustum of a Pyramid: LSA = (1/2)l(p+p'), V = (1/3)h(A+A'+√(AA')).
For a Frustum of a Right Circular Cone: LSA = πl(r+r'), V = (1/3)πh(r²+r'²+rr').

sections.section_title: Surface areas and volumes of composed solids.

slides.title: 6.4 Composed Solids
content: Definition: A solid made from two or more basic solids.
Volume: Sum of the volumes of its parts.
Surface Area: Sum of the exposed surface areas of its parts.
Important: Do not double-count the areas where parts are joined.

slides.title: 6.5 Applications of Solid Figures
content: Real-world uses of volume and surface area.
Examples:
- Determining the volume of a bucket (frustum of a cone) to find capacity.
- Calculating material cost based on total surface area (e.g., paint, canvas).
- Finding the volume of concrete needed for construction projects.
- Understanding density, capacity, and space utilization.

slides.title: Unit 7: Coordinate Geometry - Section 7.1: Distance
content: Distance Formula: d = √[(x2 - x1)² + (y2 - y1)²].
Derived from the Pythagorean Theorem.
Applies to any two points in the Cartesian plane.
For horizontal/vertical lines: d = |x2 - x1| or |y2 - y1|.

slides.title: 7.2 Division of a Line Segment
content: Section Formula: If R divides P(x1,y1) and Q(x2,y2) in the ratio p:q, then
Midpoint Formula: A special case where p = q = 1.

slides.title: 7.3 Equation of a Line
content: Slope (m): m = (y2-y1)/(x2-x1). Also m = tan θ (angle of inclination).
Point-Slope Form: y - y1 = m(x - x1).
Slope-Intercept Form: y = mx + b.
Two-Point Form: y - y1 = ((y2-y1)/(x2-x1))(x - x1).
General Form: Ax + By + C = 0.

sections.section_title: Slopes of parallel and perpendicular lines.

slides.title: 7.4 Parallel and Perpendicular Lines
content: Parallel Lines: Have the same slope (m1 = m2).
Perpendicular Lines: Slopes are negative reciprocals (m1 * m2 = -1).
Example: Lines with slopes 2 and -1/2 are perpendicular.

slides.title: 7.5 Equation of a Circle
content: Standard Form: (x - h)² + (y - k)² = r², where (h,k) is the center and r is the radius.
Center at Origin: x² + y² = r².
General Form: x² + y² + lx + my + n = 0.
Converting: Complete the square to find center and radius from the general form.

slides.title: 7.6 Applications of Coordinate Geometry
content: Area of a Triangle: A = (1/2) |x1(y2 - y3) + x2(y3 - y1) + x3(y1 - y2)|.
Used to find area from coordinates of vertices.
Classifying Triangles: Use distance formula to find side lengths (isosceles, equilateral, scalene).
Use slopes to check for right angles (perpendicular lines).
